title: Insurance claims
like: filing a car insurance claim online
brief: After a hailstorm, thousands of drivers file claims online, each with a handful of photos. The storm offer ends at 5 pm, so everyone files at the last minute. Every claim must be saved safely, and every customer gets a confirmation email.

clarify.q: Does the customer need an answer at once?
clarify.a: No. "We received your claim" is enough, and the confirmation email can follow within a minute or two.
About 3 MB each. They are evidence, so none may be lost.

clarify.q: How reliable is the email provider?
clarify.a: It takes about 1,000 emails a second but can fail for a while. A missed email is bad, a lost claim is worse.

clarify.q: What is kept for the regulator?
clarify.a: Personal data in one controlled place, encrypted, with an audit trail, and records kept for years.

notes: The storm-offer deadline is 5 pm, so load climbs for hours.
Adjusters browse claims in an internal console.

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

hints: A claim should never be lost because a helper (email, a database) is slow. Where can a claim wait safely for a moment?
Photos go straight to object storage. Claims and confirmations can go to a queue, and workers save them to the database and send the email at a steady pace.
Notification failure must not undo or duplicate an accepted claim. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The customer should never wait for anything slow. Photos land directly in object storage. Claims and confirmation emails go into a queue, so the surge becomes a longer line instead of errors, and an email outage only delays emails. Reads come from a cache over a read replica. The audit questions are answered by four small additions: audit log, key service, privacy vault and backups.

designs.name: Save first, process after
designs.why: The customer gets "received" in a fraction of a second. Photos go to object storage. A queue and workers write claims and send emails at a pace the database and the provider can take, so a partner outage costs delay, never a claim.

tradeoffs: Saving first and processing after means a claim can be accepted before a later check finds a problem. Support follows up, which is the normal process anyway.
The queue adds seconds between "received" and "saved". In return the database and the email provider never see the surge at full speed.
Photos at 3 MB each add up: 40 TB costs about $900 a month in object storage, far less than keeping them in a database.
The privacy vault costs about $1,000 a month and removes personal data from every other table, which makes the audit much easier.
editorial.realWorld: After a major storm an insurer can receive many times its normal claim volume in a day, and most photo evidence is stored as plain files in object storage (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Insurance claims: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Accept a durable claim before the cutoff and publish its confirmation reliably. Cutoff semantics need an authoritative timestamp and durable receipt. Separate object upload from atomic claim submission; unfinished objects need cleanup. Notification failure must not undo or duplicate an accepted claim.

fields.label: Step 1. A claim reaches the server just before 17:00. What proves acceptance?
options: The client clock and a queued upload
A durable server receipt with claim id and accepted_at under a stated cutoff rule
fields.explanation: Cutoff semantics need an authoritative timestamp and durable receipt.

fields.label: Step 2. The photo upload completes but claim metadata fails. What can be retried?
options: Allocate another claim for each upload attempt
Resume the same claim and attach verified object ids idempotently
fields.explanation: Separate object upload from atomic claim submission; unfinished objects need cleanup.

fields.label: Step 3. Confirmation email delivery fails after acceptance. Is the claim lost?
options: No; an outbox retries confirmation independently with the same claim id
Yes; ask the customer to file again
fields.explanation: Notification failure must not undo or duplicate an accepted claim.

correctness.responsibility: Accept a durable claim before the cutoff and publish its confirmation reliably.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 20 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $4023. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
